content: Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM), also known as chronic otitis media (COM), is a persistent condition involving inflammation and infection of the middle ear and mastoid cavity. It is characterized by ear discharge (otorrhoea) through a perforated tympanic membrane. The primary symptoms of CSOM include persistent ear discharge and hearing loss. The treatment options for CSOM include antibiotics and antiseptics, which work by either killing or inhibiting the growth of microorganisms responsible for the infection. Antibiotics can be administered either topically (directly into the ear) or systemically (via oral or injectable routes), while antiseptics are exclusively applied topically to the ear. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of antibiotics compared to antiseptics in managing CSOM. The research included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a minimum follow-up period of one week. Participants included both adults and children with chronic ear discharge lasting more than two weeks, either due to CSOM or an unknown cause. The interventions studied were either single or combined antibiotic agents, applied topically (without steroids) or systemically, compared to single or combined topical antiseptic agents, which were administered as ear drops, powders, irrigations, or as part of aural toileting procedures. The primary outcomes assessed were the resolution of ear discharge (or achieving a dry ear), health-related quality of life, and ear pain or discomfort. Secondary outcomes included hearing improvement, serious complications, and ototoxicity. The evidence was graded using the GRADE system to determine the certainty of the findings. Seven studies involving 935 participants were included in the analysis. These studies compared antibiotics with various antiseptics, including acetic acid, aluminum acetate, boric acid, and povidone-iodine. None of the studies reported outcomes related to quality of life or serious complications. 1. Acetic acid versus topical antibiotics (quinolones or aminoglycosides): The evidence is very uncertain regarding whether acetic acid is as effective as aminoglycosides in resolving ear discharge within one to two weeks (risk ratio [RR] 0.88, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.72 to 1.08; 1 study; 100 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No data were available for ear discharge resolution beyond four weeks. It is also very uncertain whether acetic acid causes more ear pain, discomfort, or local irritation compared to topical antibiotics (RR 0.16, 95% CI 0.02 to 1.34; 2 RCTs; 189 participants; very low-certainty evidence). No significant differences were reported for hearing outcomes (quinolones) or suspected ototoxicity (aminoglycosides), but the evidence was of very low certainty. 2. Aluminum acetate versus topical antibiotics: No usable results were available from the single study comparing aluminum acetate with topical antibiotics. 3. Boric acid versus topical antibiotics (quinolones): One study found that topical antibiotics (quinolones) were more effective than boric acid in resolving ear discharge within one to two weeks (RR 1.86, 95% CI 1.48 to 2.35; 1 study; 411 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). This suggests that for every four people treated with topical antibiotics, one additional person would achieve resolution of ear discharge compared to boric acid. No data were available for ear discharge resolution beyond four weeks. Hearing improvement was greater in the topical antibiotic group compared to the boric acid group (mean difference [MD] 2.79 decibels [dB], 95% CI 0.48 to 5.10; 1 study; 390 participants; low-certainty evidence), but the clinical significance of this difference is uncertain. Boric acid may cause more ear pain, discomfort, or irritation compared to quinolones (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.98; 2 studies; 510 participants; low-certainty evidence). Suspected ototoxicity was not reported. 4. Povidone-iodine versus topical antibiotics (quinolones): It is uncertain whether there is a difference in the resolution of ear discharge between povidone-iodine and quinolones at one to two weeks (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.26; 1 RCT; 39 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The study qualitatively reported no differences in hearing outcomes or ototoxic effects between the two groups, but the evidence was of very low certainty. No data were available for ear discharge resolution beyond four weeks, or for ear pain, discomfort, or irritation. 5. Acetic acid with aural toileting versus topical and systemic antibiotics (quinolones): One study reported that participants receiving acetic acid ear drops combined with aural toileting (suction clearance every two days) had a higher resolution of ear discharge at one month compared to those receiving both topical and oral antibiotics (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.90; 100 participants). No data were available for ear discharge resolution at one to two weeks, ear pain, discomfort, irritation, hearing outcomes, or suspected ototoxicity. Conclusions: The use of topical antibiotics (quinolones) likely leads to a higher resolution of ear discharge compared to boric acid within two weeks. However, there is limited evidence regarding the effectiveness of other topical antibiotics or antiseptics, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions. Adverse events were not consistently reported across studies.
